pos: n. pl. (soles bound to the foot with thongs; the footwear of the Twelve and of Peter's deliverance)
etymology: Greek sandalion, a small board, through Latin. The Authorized Version uses the word twice, both in the New Testament: in the Lord's instructions to the Twelve and in the angel's instructions to Peter in the prison.
biblical_def: But be shod with sandals; and not put on two coats. The Lord is sending out the Twelve two by two, and the outfitting is deliberately meagre: nothing for the journey save a staff only, no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse, and one coat apiece. Sandals are permitted because a man must walk; a second coat is not, because a second coat is a margin against depending on God and on the households that receive them. The other occurrence is in a prison at night. The angel said unto him, Gird thyself, and bind on thy sandals. And so he did. And he saith unto him, Cast thy garment about thee, and follow me. Peter is chained between two soldiers, the church is praying in Mary's house, and the rescue proceeds through an ordinary sequence of getting dressed. Even in a miracle a man ties his own shoes. The two passages together hold the dictionary's doctrine of ordinary means and extraordinary grace in one homely object, and Paul supplies the figure that gathers them: your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a kind of shoe, consisting of a sole fastened to the foot; in Scripture, the footwear permitted to the Twelve and bound on by Peter at his deliverance.
webster_full: SANDAL, n. A kind of shoe, consisting of a sole fastened to the foot with strings or thongs.
SHOD, pp. Furnished with shoes; having shoes on the feet.
SCRIP, n. A small bag; a wallet; a satchel carried by travellers and shepherds.
GIRD, v.t. To bind by surrounding with any flexible substance, as a belt or cord.
PROVISION, n. The act of providing or making previous preparation; measures taken beforehand.
scriptures: Mar 6:9
But be shod with sandals; and not put on two coats.
Mar 6:8
And commanded them that they should take nothing for their journey, save a staff only; no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse.
Act 12:8
And the angel said unto him, Gird thyself, and bind on thy sandals. And so he did. And he saith unto him, Cast thy garment about thee, and follow me.
Eph 6:15
And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace;
corruption_summary: The mission instructions of Mark 6 are taken either as a rule of permanent poverty binding on every minister or as a quaint detail with no application; the Lord gave them for a particular sending and himself revised the terms later.
corruption_paragraphs: The Twelve were sent out with a staff and sandals and no bread, and they lacked nothing. But in Luke 22 the Lord asks them, when I sent you without purse, and scrip, and shoes, lacked ye any thing? And they said, Nothing. And then he says, But now, he that hath a purse, let him take it, and likewise his scrip. The same Lord who stripped them down re-equipped them for a different season. A rule read out of Mark 6 as a permanent law of ministerial destitution ignores that revision, and a reading that finds nothing binding in it ignores the principle underneath, which is that the labourer is worthy of his hire and that God provides for the men he sends through the people he sends them to.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, and the principle to recover is dependence without presumption. Peter's night in prison shows the same balance from the other side: God sends an angel, opens the iron gate of his own accord, and still tells the man to put his shoes on and walk. The church meanwhile is praying and does not believe the answer when it knocks at the door. Ordinary obedience and extraordinary deliverance are not rivals in Scripture; they are almost always found in the same room.

“Gird thyself, and bind on thy sandals” — the angel's words in the prison.
“your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace” — the armour figure.

pos: n. (a set of garments; also a petition or legal cause)
etymology: From Old French suite, a following, from Latin sequi, to follow — things that go together, whether garments in a set or a cause pursued at law. The Authorized Version uses both senses.
biblical_def: The clothing sense appears in one of the strangest transactions in Scripture. Micah, a man of mount Ephraim with a house of gods and a homemade ephod, hires a wandering Levite: I will give thee ten shekels of silver by the year, and a suit of apparel, and thy victuals. So the Levite went in. A salary, a uniform, and board, and a priesthood purchased at a fixed rate. Micah's conclusion is one of the most self-deceived sentences in the Old Testament: Now know I that the LORD will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest. He had broken the second commandment with the images, the regulative principle with the shrine, and the law of the priesthood with the appointment, and he read his own arrangement as a guarantee of blessing. The frame the book puts around it is the refrain of Judges: in those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes. The legal sense of the word appears in Absalom's campaign for the throne, promising justice to every man which hath any suit or cause, and in Job, where many shall make suit unto the restored man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a set of things used together, as a suit of clothes; also, the prosecution of a claim, a petition, an entreaty.
webster_full: SUIT, n. A set; a number of things used together, and in a degree necessary to be united; as a suit of clothes.
SUIT, n. The act of suing; the process by which one endeavors to gain an end or an object.
SUIT, n. Petition; entreaty; solicitation; a request made to a superior.
APPAREL, n. Clothing; vesture; garments; dress.
HIRE, n. The price, reward or compensation paid for personal service.
scriptures: And Micah said unto him, Dwell with me, and be unto me a father and a priest, and I will give thee ten shekels of silver by the year, and a suit of apparel, and thy victuals. So the Levite went in. a
Jdg 17:6
In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
Then said Micah, Now know I that the LORD will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest.
Absalom said moreover, Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!
corruption_summary: Worship is arranged according to what seems right and reverent to the worshipper, and its sincerity taken as its warrant; Judges 17 shows a devout man building exactly that and reading it as the LORD's favour.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah is not an atheist. He is religious, generous with silver, eager to have a Levite rather than his own son in the office, and convinced that God will do him good. Every element of his worship is invented and every element is sincere. This is precisely why the Reformed tradition holds the regulative principle: that what God has not commanded in his worship is not permitted, however devout the intention. Sincerity is not a warrant, and the second commandment forbids worshipping the true God by images of our own devising as firmly as it forbids false gods.

The refrain of the book supplies the diagnosis and it is political as well as religious: there was no king in Israel, and every man did that which was right in his own eyes. Where no authority is acknowledged, each man's conscience becomes his own liturgy committee, and Judges spends its closing chapters showing where that ends. A suit of apparel and ten shekels a year bought Micah a chaplain, and the Danites took chaplain, ephod, and images away from him by force a chapter later, which is the usual fate of a religion a man has made himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'erek beged (H6187, H899), an order or set of garments; riyb (H7379), a suit or cause at law; chalah (H2470), to entreat or make suit.

Hebrew chalah (H2470) — to be weak, to entreat, to make suit; many shall make suit unto thee.

“every man which hath any suit or cause” — the legal sense, in Absalom's campaign.
“Now know I that the LORD will do me good” — sincerity mistaken for warrant.

pos: n. (the neck-band of a coat; in Job, the disease that binds like one)
etymology: From Latin collare, a band for the neck, from collum, neck. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Job's lament, where his disease has changed his garment and binds him about as the collar of his coat.
biblical_def: By the great force of my disease is my garment changed: it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat. Job is describing what the sickness has done to his own skin, and he reaches for a piece of clothing to say it: the thing is not upon him, it is around him, close and constricting at the throat, like the neck of a garment that no longer fits. Two chapters earlier he had used clothing for the opposite condition: I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem. The same man in the same book is clothed twice, once in the respect of the city gate and once in the disease that has replaced it. Between the two lies everything the book is about. He does not deny the change, minimise it, or make peace with it prematurely: he hath cast me into the mire, and I am become like dust and ashes; my harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep. Scripture gives a suffering man this vocabulary on purpose. Lament is not unbelief, and Job is vindicated at the end of the book against the friends who wanted his complaints tidied away.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): something worn round the neck, as a ring of metal or the part of a garment which surrounds the neck; in Scripture, the figure Job uses for his binding disease.
webster_full: COLLAR, n. Something worn round the neck, as a ring of metal, or a chain.
COLLAR, n. The part of a garment which surrounds the neck.
DISEASE, n. In a general sense, pain, uneasiness, distress; any deviation from health.
LAMENT, v.i. To mourn; to grieve; to weep or wail; to express sorrow.
AFFLICTION, n. The cause of continued pain of body or mind, as sickness, losses, calamity, adversity.
scriptures: By the great force of my disease is my garment changed: it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat.
I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem.
He hath cast me into the mire, and I am become like dust and ashes.
My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep.
corruption_summary: Suffering is handled either with therapeutic vocabulary that treats it as a wound to be processed or with a false piety that forbids complaint; Job's language is given in Scripture as a sanctioned register for grief before God.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of modern counsel about affliction has borrowed a vocabulary that Scripture does not use and abandoned the one it does. The Bible's categories for Job's condition are suffering, affliction, the hand of God, the breaking of a man under a curse he did not personally earn, and the language it gives him is blunt and physical — the collar of his coat, the mire, dust and ashes, the harp turned to mourning. That vocabulary is more honest than the clinical one and far more honest than the pious one that hurries a sufferer past the lament to the application.

The other corruption is the friends' and it is the one God rebukes by name. They could not tolerate an unexplained affliction and so they explained it, and every explanation was an accusation. At the end the LORD said to Eliphaz, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath. The man who complained bitterly and would not curse God is the one commended. The dictionary takes that as its rule for the ministry of comfort: sit seven days, speak little, and never explain what God has not explained.

pos: n. pl. (ornamental bands or sashes for the head; among the finery Isaiah lists for removal)
etymology: From head and band. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, in the long inventory of the ornaments of the daughters of Zion which the Lord promises to take away.
biblical_def: The bonnets, and the ornaments of the legs, and the headbands, and the tablets, and the earrings. Isaiah is reciting a wardrobe, twenty-one items over four verses, with the patience of an auctioneer, and every item is going. The reason is given before the list begins and it is not fashion but posture: because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet. The sin named is not ornament but haughtiness displayed through ornament, a whole manner of moving through a city designed to be looked at. And the sentence is an exchange, item for item: instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty. The chapter ends with the city itself sitting on the ground. The New Testament makes the same point without the catalogue: whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a fillet or band worn about the head; in Scripture, among the ornaments of the daughters of Zion which the Lord takes away.
webster_full: HEADBAND, n. A fillet; a band for the head; also, the band at each end of a book.
FILLET, n. A little band to tie about the hair of the head.
BRAVERY, n. Show; splendor; magnificence; showy dress; in Scripture, the finery of ornament.
HAUGHTY, a. Proud and disdainful; having a high opinion of one's self, with contempt of others.
MODESTY, n. That lowly temper which accompanies a moderate estimate of one's own worth.
scriptures: Isa 3:20
The bonnets, and the ornaments of the legs, and the headbands, and the tablets, and the earrings,
Isa 3:16
Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:
Isa 3:24

And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty.
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
corruption_summary: Modesty is reduced to a rule about hemlines, or dismissed altogether as body-policing; Isaiah names the sin in the walk and the eyes before he names a single garment, and Peter locates the true adorning in the hidden man of the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 3 is often quoted as a dress code and it is not one. The indictment is delivered before the inventory: haughty, with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go. The ornaments are evidence, not the offence. This is why a mechanical standard of measurement never produces the virtue it aims at; it can be kept exactly by a heart that is doing precisely what Isaiah describes, and it can condemn a woman who is doing nothing of the kind. The biblical category is the display of self where the display of God is owed.

Peter completes the teaching rather than contradicting it. He forbids making the outward the adorning and then names what is: the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. Paul's parallel adds shamefacedness and sobriety, and then good works, which he calls the apparel that becometh women professing godliness. So the dictionary teaches modesty as a doctrine of the heart with real consequences for the wardrobe, and refuses both the legalism that inverts the order and the modern claim that clothing carries no moral weight at all.

pos: n. pl. (head coverings; part of the dress of the three Hebrews cast into the furnace)
etymology: Old English haet, a covering for the head. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, in Daniel, listing what Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were wearing when they were bound and thrown into the fire.
biblical_def: Then these men were bound in their coats, their hosen, and their hats, and their other garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace. The clothing is listed for a reason, and the reason comes out twelve verses later when the officials inspect the three men: the fire had no power over their bodies, nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them. The garments named going in are the garments checked coming out. Only one thing burned, and it was the ropes. The confession that put them in the furnace is the one the dictionary keeps as the model of faith without bargaining: our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up. They did not know they would be spared. They refused on the ground of the second commandment and left the outcome with God. And the king, looking in, said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a covering for the head; in Scripture, part of the dress of the three Hebrews, named going into the furnace and found unharmed coming out.
webster_full: HAT, n. A covering for the head; a garment made of different materials, and worn by men or women.
HOSEN, n. pl. The old plural of hose; stockings or breeches.
FURNACE, n. A place where a vehement fire is maintained for melting ores or other purposes.
CONFESSION, n. The acknowledgment of a crime, fault, or something to one's disadvantage; open declaration of faith.
DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint.
scriptures: Dan 3:21
Then these men were bound in their coats, their hosen, and their hats, and their other garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace.
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
Dan 3:25
He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God.
Dan 3:27

And the princes, governors, and captains, and the king's counsellors, being gathered together, saw these men, upon whose bodies the fire had no power, nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them.
corruption_summary: Faith is measured by the confidence that God will grant the deliverance asked for, so that an unanswered prayer is read as insufficient faith; the three Hebrews confess God's power to deliver and then say but if not, and are commended.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 3:18 is the sentence that separates biblical faith from the teaching that makes certainty of outcome the measure of belief. Our God is able to deliver us, and he will deliver us — then, immediately, but if not, we still will not bow. The confidence is in God's power and God's right, not in a guaranteed result, and the refusal to worship is not conditional on the rescue. Where faith is defined as an inner certainty that produces the desired outcome, every sufferer who is not delivered is left with a second accusation on top of the first, and Hebrews 11 flatly contradicts it by listing, in the same chapter and the same breath, those who escaped the edge of the sword and those who were sawn asunder.

The second matter in the chapter is the ground of the refusal, which was not conscience in the modern sense but the commandment. Nebuchadnezzar demanded an act of worship toward an image, and the second commandment forbids it, so the answer was fixed before the furnace was heated. Christians are called to obey the magistrate in his sphere and to refuse him at exactly the point where he claims what belongs to God. The three said so in nine words and let the king do what he could, and the fourth man in the fire is the dictionary's comfort for everyone who has had to say it since.

pos: adj. (clothed; covered as with a garment)
etymology: The old past participle of clothe. The Authorized Version uses it twice: of Ahijah the Shilonite wearing the new garment he was about to tear into twelve pieces, and of the LORD himself clad with zeal as a cloke.
biblical_def: The first use sets up a prophetic sign. Ahijah the Shilonite found Jeroboam in the way, and he had clad himself with a new garment, and they two were alone in the field. He caught the new garment and rent it in twelve pieces and told Jeroboam to take ten, for thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon. The garment is new, which is the point: a kingdom at its height, whole and freshly made, torn up in a field with nobody watching. The second use is one of the most striking pictures of God in Isaiah: he put on righteousness as a breastplate, and an helmet of salvation upon his head; and he put on the garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a cloke. God arms himself because there is no man to intercede, and the armour he wears is his own character — righteousness, salvation, vengeance, zeal. Paul takes that same armoury and puts it on the church in Ephesians 6, and gives the shortest command about clothing in the Bible: put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): clothed; invested; covered as with a garment; the old participle of clothe.
webster_full: CLAD, pp. of clothe. Clothed; invested; covered as with a garment.
CLOTHE, v.t. To put on garments; to invest with raiment; to cover with dress.
CLOKE, n. A loose outer garment worn over other clothes.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; ardor in the pursuit of a good cause.
BREASTPLATE, n. Armor for the breast; in Scripture, a figure of righteousness as defence.
scriptures: For he put on righteousness as a breastplate, and an helmet of salvation upon his head; and he put on the garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a cloke.

And it came to pass at that time when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, that the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him in the way; and he had clad himself with a new garment; and they two were alone in the field:
And he said to Jeroboam, Take thee ten pieces: for thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel, Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee:
But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.
corruption_summary: Divine zeal and vengeance are treated as unworthy of God and edited out of his character, leaving a deity of unmixed mildness; Isaiah 59 has him putting on vengeance and zeal precisely because there was no man to intercede.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 59:17 is inconvenient to the modern portrait of God and was never inconvenient to the church that wrote the creeds. He sees that there is no judgment, that truth is fallen in the street, that equity cannot enter, that he who departeth from evil maketh himself a prey — and it displeased him. The arming follows. A God who could survey that and remain unmoved would not be good; his zeal is the form his goodness takes toward evil, and his vengeance is the vindication of the oppressed. Scripture never presents wrath as a lapse in God's love but as its necessary edge, and the same passage ends with the Redeemer coming to Zion and a covenant that will not depart.

The second corruption is human zeal without the rest of the armour. Paul says of his countrymen that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge, and Jehu is the standing Old Testament example of a man who was very zealous for the LORD and served himself. That is why Isaiah lists the pieces together — righteousness, salvation, vengeance, zeal — and why Paul's command is not put on zeal but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ. The garment is a Person.

“was clad with zeal as a cloke” — God arming himself in Isaiah 59.
“put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ” — the garment commanded of the Christian.

etymology: From leather with the old adjectival ending -en, as in wooden and golden. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the girdle John the Baptist wore about his loins.
biblical_def: And the same John had his raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey. The description is not incidental colour. It is a deliberate quotation of Elijah, whom the men of Ahaziah described as an hairy man, girt with a girdle of leather about his loins, and it announced John's office before he opened his mouth: the prophet promised in Malachi, come in the spirit and power of Elias. Everything about the clothing says wilderness rather than court. The Lord made the contrast himself: What went ye out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken with the wind? But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? behold, they that wear soft clothing are in kings' houses. John was not in a king's house; he was eventually in a king's prison, for telling that king the truth about his brother's wife. His message was four words long and it has never been improved: Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. And the Lord's verdict on him is the highest given to any man born of woman, with a sting in its tail for the least in the kingdom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): made of leather; consisting of leather; in Scripture, the girdle of John the Baptist, worn after the manner of Elijah.

LEATHER, n. The skin of an animal dressed and prepared for use.
GIRDLE, n. A band or belt; something drawn round the waist of a person and tied or buckled.
RAIMENT, n. Clothing in general; vestments; vesture; garments.
FORERUNNER, n. A messenger sent before to give notice of the approach of another.

And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
Mat 11:8
But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? behold, they that wear soft clothing are in kings' houses.
Verily I say unto you, Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
corruption_summary: Repentance is softened into a change of perspective or a general spiritual openness, and the preacher who names sin is judged harsh; John's office, dress, diet and message were all a standing refusal of that softening.
corruption_paragraphs: John's preaching is the pattern the dictionary keeps for the ministry of repentance. He called the religious leaders a generation of vipers and asked who had warned them to flee from the wrath to come; he told the multitudes to bring forth fruits meet for repentance; he gave the publicans and the soldiers specific, concrete instructions about money and violence; and he told Herod that it was not lawful for him to have his brother's wife, which cost him his head. Repentance in Scripture is a turning that shows, with fruit attached, and no part of John's ministry supports the idea that naming a particular sin to a particular man is unloving.

The clothing carries the argument silently. Soft raiment belongs in kings' houses; camel's hair and a leathern girdle belong in the wilderness where a man has nothing to lose and no patron to please. A ministry that has arranged its comforts inside the palace will find it very difficult to say the sentence John said to Herod. And yet the Lord's verdict keeps even John in proportion: he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he — not because John was small, but because the kingdom he announced is that great.
roots_summary: Greek dermatinos (G1193), made of skin or leather; zone (G2223), a girdle or belt; metanoeo (G3340), to repent, to change the mind.
roots_lines: Greek dermatinos (G1193) — made of hide or leather; the leathern girdle of Matthew 3:4.
Greek zone (G2223) — a belt or girdle worn about the loins.
Greek endyma (G1742) — a garment, raiment; his raiment of camel's hair.
Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to change the mind, to repent; Repent ye.
Greek malakos (G3120) — soft, delicate; a man clothed in soft raiment.
usage: “a leathern girdle about his loins” — the single occurrence, of John the Baptist.
“they that wear soft clothing are in kings' houses” — the contrast the Lord drew.
“Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” — the message the dress announced.

pos: n. pl. (cloths carried from Paul's body to the sick at Ephesus)
etymology: From hand and kerchief, itself from Old French couvrechief, a head covering. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, in Luke's account of the special miracles God wrought by the hands of Paul at Ephesus.
biblical_def: And God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul: so that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them. Luke is careful with the grammar, and the care is doctrine. God wrought, by the hands of Paul, and the miracles are called special — literally, not the ordinary sort — which means Luke himself flags them as exceptional rather than exemplary. The account continues immediately into its own commentary. Certain vagabond Jews, exorcists, tried to use the name as a technique, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth, and the evil spirit answered, Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye? and the man leapt on them and overcame them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. The name is not a formula. The chapter ends where Luke wants it: fear fell on them all, the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified, many burned their books of curious arts, and so mightily grew the word of God and prevailed. The cloths were a sign; the growing word was the result.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a piece of cloth carried about the person for wiping the face; in Scripture, cloths from Paul's body by which God wrought special miracles at Ephesus.
webster_full: HANDKERCHIEF, n. A piece of cloth, usually silk or linen, carried about the person for wiping the face.
APRON, n. A cloth or piece of leather worn on the fore part of the body, to keep the clothes clean.
MIRACLE, n. In theology, an effect above human or natural power, performed in attestation of some truth.
EXORCIST, n. One who pretends to expel evil spirits by conjuration, prayers and ceremonies.
SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; belief in the direct agency of superior powers in extraordinary events.
scriptures: So that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them.
Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.
Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed.
corruption_summary: The handkerchiefs of Acts 19 are turned into a method — anointed cloths sold or mailed as vehicles of healing — when Luke calls the miracles special and follows them immediately with the story of men who tried to use the name as a technique and were beaten for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The prayer-cloth industry rests on this verse and the chapter refutes it in the next breath. Luke marks the miracles as not-the-ordinary-kind, and then narrates what happens when men treat spiritual power as a portable method: the sons of Sceva are stripped and wounded by the very spirit they tried to command. Between those two paragraphs lies the whole difference between God working sovereignly through an apostle to attest the gospel at a pagan capital, and a technique sold to the desperate. The cloths healed because God wrought; nothing is said about the cloths having anything in them.

The city's response shows what the miracles were for. Ephesus was a centre of curious arts, and the men who had practised them brought their books together and burned them publicly at a cost of fifty thousand pieces of silver — not sold, burned, because the money was not the point and the books were not to circulate. That is what an encounter with the true power does to the occult trade. The dictionary holds the cessationist position on the sign-gifts with the Reformed tradition, and this chapter is one of the reasons: the signs attested the apostles, and the apostolic office closed with them, and what remains and grows is the word.
roots_summary: Greek soudarion (G4676), a napkin or handkerchief; simikinthion (G4612), an apron; dunamis (G1411), power, and so a mighty work.
roots_lines: Greek soudarion (G4676) — a face-cloth, a napkin; also the napkin about the Lord's head in the tomb.
Greek simikinthion (G4612) — a workman's apron; the other cloth named at Ephesus.
Greek dunamis (G1411) — power, a mighty work; God wrought special miracles.
Greek tuchon (from G5177) — ordinary, common; the word Luke negates in calling them special.
Greek horkizo (G3726) — to adjure, to bind by an oath; We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.
usage: “from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons” — the single occurrence.
“Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?” — the answer to the name used as technique.
“So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed” — the outcome Luke records.

pos: n. (the joint between foot and leg; the old spelling of ankle)
etymology: Old English ancleow, the joint of the foot. The Authorized Version spells it ancle, and uses it of the bones that received strength in the healing at the Beautiful gate.
biblical_def: And he took him by the right hand, and lifted him up: and immediately his feet and ancle bones received strength. The man was above forty years old, lame from his mother's womb, carried daily and laid at the gate called Beautiful to ask alms. Luke, a physician, names the part that changed. What Peter offered first was a refusal: Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk. The apostles had nothing the beggar was asking for and everything he needed. And the man's response is one of the most exuberant sentences in Acts — he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God. The healing became the occasion of Peter's sermon in Solomon's porch and of his defence before the council, where he stated the exclusive claim that the whole book rests on: neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved. A pair of ancle bones is where that sermon started.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the joint which connects the foot with the leg; spelled ancle in the Authorized Version.
webster_full: ANCLE, n. The joint which connects the foot with the leg.
LAME, a. Crippled or disabled in a limb, or otherwise injured so as to be unsound and impaired in strength.
ALMS, n. Any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor, as money, food, or clothing.
BEAUTIFUL, a. Having the qualities which constitute beauty; in Scripture, the name of a gate of the temple.
SALVATION, n. The redemption of man from the bondage of sin and liability to eternal death.
scriptures: Act 3:7
And he took him by the right hand, and lifted him up: and immediately his feet and ancle bones received strength.
Act 3:6
Then Peter said, Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk.
Act 3:8
And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
corruption_summary: The exclusivity of Acts 4:12 is set aside as culturally conditioned, so that the name which healed the lame man becomes one path among several; Peter preached it to the very council with power to kill him.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved. The sentence is spoken by a fisherman standing before the Sanhedrin, under arrest, with the healed man visible beside him, and it is the sentence that modern pluralism most wants edited. Every softening runs into the setting: Peter had nothing to gain by exclusivity and everything to lose, and the rulers could not deny the miracle and could only command them not to speak at all in this name. The claim is either true or it is the grossest presumption; it was never a polite cultural preference.

The corruption inside the church takes a gentler form, which is to affirm the doctrine and stop preaching the name. Peter's method at the Beautiful gate is instructive here too. He did not begin with the crowd's question, he began with what he had, and he named Jesus Christ of Nazareth to a beggar who had asked only for money. And when the people ran together in amazement he immediately turned their eyes off himself: why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk? The healing was a signpost and Peter refused to stand in front of it.
roots_summary: Greek sphudron (G4974), the ankle bone; basis (G939), the foot, that on which one steps; stereoo (G4732), to make firm or strengthen.
roots_lines: Greek sphudron (G4974) — the ankle bone; the one occurrence, Acts 3:7.
Greek basis (G939) — a step, and so the foot; his feet and ancle bones.
Greek stereoo (G4732) — to make solid, to strengthen; received strength.
Greek hallomai (G242) — to leap, to spring up; walking, and leaping, and praising God.
Greek sozo (G4982) — to save, to heal, to make whole; whereby we must be saved.
usage: “his feet and ancle bones received strength” — the single occurrence.
“Silver and gold have I none” — what the apostles could not give.
“there is none other name under heaven” — where the healing led.

pos: adj. (in crisping pins, instruments for curling the hair, or ornamented purses)
etymology: From crisp, Latin crispus, curled. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the phrase crisping pins, among the finery of the daughters of Zion; the Hebrew word also denotes an ornamented bag or purse.
biblical_def: The changeable suits of apparel, and the mantles, and the wimples, and the crisping pins. The verse sits at the end of Isaiah's inventory, and the crisping pins close it. The whole catalogue begins with an announcement of removal: in that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon, and then twenty more items over the following verses. The Hebrew word here is used elsewhere of a bag or purse, which is why the older commentators divide between curling irons and ornamented pouches; either way it belongs to the same wardrobe of display. What the passage is measuring is not the price of the goods but the direction of the heart, and Isaiah has already given the diagnosis in verse 16. The chapter ends with the city stripped and sitting on the ground: and her gates shall lament and mourn; and she being desolate shall sit upon the ground. Paul gives the positive rule for the church in one verse: that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): curling; forming into curls or ringlets; crisping pins, instruments for curling the hair, or, as some render the Hebrew, ornamented purses.
webster_full: CRISP, v.t. To curl; to form into ringlets, as hair; to wreathe or interweave.
CRISPING-PIN, n. An instrument for curling the hair; rendered by some a purse or bag.
WIMPLE, n. A hood or veil; a covering for the neck, formerly worn by women.
MANTLE, n. A kind of cloke or loose garment worn over the other garments.
SOBRIETY, n. Habitual soberness or temperance; seriousness; gravity; freedom from inordinate passion.
scriptures: Isa 3:22
The changeable suits of apparel, and the mantles, and the wimples, and the crisping pins,
Isa 3:18
In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon,
Isa 3:26
And her gates shall lament and mourn; and she being desolate shall sit upon the ground.
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
corruption_summary: Luxury is defended as a private matter of taste while the poor of the same city go unrelieved; Isaiah's catalogue of finery comes immediately after his charge that the rulers have ground the faces of the poor.
corruption_paragraphs: The finery of Isaiah 3 is not indicted in a vacuum. A few verses earlier the LORD stands up to plead and enters into judgment with the ancients of his people and the princes: ye have eaten up the vineyard; the spoil of the poor is in your houses. What mean ye that ye beat my people to pieces, and grind the faces of the poor? Only then does the catalogue of ornaments begin. The crisping pins are the visible end of an economy that had been taking from the wrong people, and the prophet lets the wardrobe testify about the accounts.

The New Testament keeps the connection. Paul's instruction about modest apparel names costly array alongside broided hair and gold and pearls, and then finishes the sentence with the alternative: but which becometh women professing godliness with good works. Adorning is not abolished, it is redirected — the ornament is the works. James makes the same point with a man in goodly apparel walking into an assembly and being given the best seat while a poor man in vile raiment is told to stand. The dictionary treats luxury as a question about neighbours and not only about taste.
roots_summary: Hebrew chariyt (H2754), a bag or purse, rendered crisping pin; machalatsah (H4254), a change of raiment; mitpachath (H4304), a veil or wimple.
roots_lines: Hebrew chariyt (H2754) — a bag or pouch, rendered crisping pin; also the bags of 2 Kings 5:23.
Hebrew machalatsah (H4254) — a robe of state, a change of raiment; the changeable suits of apparel.
Hebrew mitpachath (H4304) — a wide cloak, a veil; the wimples.
Hebrew ma'ataphah (H4595) — an overcoat or mantle; the mantles.
Greek katastole (G2689) — apparel, deportment; in modest apparel.
usage: “the wimples, and the crisping pins” — the single occurrence, closing Isaiah's inventory.
“the bravery of their tinkling ornaments” — how the catalogue opens.
“she being desolate shall sit upon the ground” — how the chapter ends.
